questions.stem: Why do phospholipids form a bilayer when placed in water?

options.text: The cell uses ATP to arrange them tail to tail
options.why: No energy is spent building it. The bilayer forms on its own because of how the molecule interacts with water.

options.text: Hydrophilic heads face water and hydrophobic tails are shielded
options.why: The heads interact with the water on both sides, and the tails end up in the center, away from it.

options.text: Water pushes the tails together with a repulsive force
options.why: Nothing pushes. Water molecules bond with each other and the heads, and that leaves the tails together.

options.text: Covalent bonds form between tails in the two layers
options.why: The two layers aren't bonded together. Hydrophobic interactions hold the tails in the middle.

questions.stem: Which of these crosses the phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion?

options.text: Sodium ions
options.why: Ions are charged, so they need a channel or a pump to get through.

options.text: Glucose
options.why: Glucose is large and polar, so it crosses through a carrier protein.

options.text: Oxygen
options.why: Oxygen is small and non-polar, so it passes straight through the hydrophobic core.

options.text: Amino acids
options.why: Amino acids are charged or polar, so they need transport proteins.

questions.stem: Why can't ions cross the phospholipid bilayer directly?

options.text: The hydrophobic core repels charged particles
options.why: That's the trap. The core doesn't push ions away. Moving a charge into a non-polar region costs too much energy.

options.text: Moving a charged ion into the non-polar core is energetically unfavorable
options.why: An ion interacts well with water and not at all with the tails, so it stays out of the core.

options.text: Ions are too large to fit between the phospholipids
options.why: Many ions are smaller than oxygen or water molecules. Charge is the problem, not size.

options.text: The phosphate heads bond permanently to any ion
options.why: The heads don't trap ions. The barrier is the hydrophobic core.

options.text: Through a channel or carrier protein, down the gradient, without ATP
options.why: The protein gives a route through the membrane. The gradient supplies the energy, so no ATP is spent.

options.text: Through a pump protein, down the gradient, using ATP to speed it up
options.why: Facilitated diffusion never uses ATP. If you give it an ATP cost, the examiner reads it as active transport.

options.text: Directly through the bilayer, down the gradient, without any proteins
options.why: That's simple diffusion. "Facilitated" means a protein helps.

options.text: Through a channel protein, against the gradient, powered by ATP
options.why: Moving against a gradient needs energy, and that's active transport.

questions.stem: What makes a transport process active?

options.text: It moves a substance through a membrane protein
options.why: Facilitated diffusion uses proteins too. Protein use doesn't make it active.

options.text: It moves a substance against its gradient using energy
options.why: Energy, usually ATP, is spent to move something from low concentration to high.

options.text: It moves a substance faster than simple diffusion
options.why: Speed doesn't define it. Aquaporins speed up osmosis and that's still passive.

options.text: It moves water toward a lower water potential
options.why: That's osmosis, which is passive.

options.text: Let water cross a membrane it otherwise couldn't cross
options.why: Water can cross the bilayer without them, only slowly. Aquaporins speed it up.

options.text: Speed up osmosis without using any ATP
options.why: They're channels that greatly increase permeability to water. They change the rate, not the direction.

options.text: Pump water against its gradient using ATP
options.why: Aquaporins are channels, not pumps. Water still moves toward the lower water potential.

options.text: Reverse the direction of osmosis when needed
options.why: Direction is set by the water potential difference. Aquaporins only change how fast it happens.

questions.stem: What does cholesterol do to an animal cell membrane?

options.text: Makes the membrane more fluid at every temperature
options.why: It works in both directions. Giving only one effect is a common way to drop the mark.

options.text: Makes the membrane more rigid at every temperature
options.why: At low temperatures it does the opposite and stops the membrane from becoming too rigid.

options.text: Carries ions across the membrane by diffusion
options.why: Cholesterol isn't a transport molecule. Its job is fluidity.

options.text: Limits fluidity when warm and prevents stiffening when cold
options.why: Cholesterol buffers fluidity. It restrains phospholipids when warm and stops them packing tightly when cold.

questions.stem: Why does a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acid tails keep a membrane fluid at low temperatures?

options.text: Kinks from double bonds stop the tails packing closely
options.why: Cis double bonds bend the tails. Bent tails can't line up tightly, so the membrane stays fluid.

options.text: Unsaturated tails are longer, so they move around more
options.why: Length isn't the point. The double bonds cause kinks, and kinks prevent close packing.

options.text: Unsaturated tails are hydrophilic, so they attract water
options.why: Unsaturated tails are still hydrophobic. They sit in the core like the saturated ones.

options.text: Double bonds release heat that warms the membrane
options.why: Double bonds don't generate heat. They change the tails' shape.

questions.stem: In one cycle of the sodium–potassium pump, which ions move and in which direction?

options.text: Three Na+ move in and two K+ move out
options.why: That's reversed. Sodium is pumped out of the cell and potassium in.

options.text: Two Na+ move out and three K+ move in
options.why: The numbers are swapped. It's three sodium out, two potassium in.

options.text: Three Na+ move out and two K+ move in
options.why: One ATP per cycle moves three sodium out and two potassium in, both against their gradients.

options.text: Three Na+ and two K+ both move out
options.why: It's an exchange. Sodium goes out and potassium comes in.

questions.stem: In sodium-dependent glucose cotransport, where is ATP hydrolyzed?

options.text: At the cotransporter, every time it moves a glucose
options.why: That's the trap. The cotransporter uses no ATP itself. It uses the sodium gradient.

options.text: At the sodium–potassium pump that builds the Na+ gradient
options.why: The pump spends ATP making the sodium gradient. Sodium flowing back through the cotransporter drags glucose with it.

options.text: Nowhere, since glucose moves down its own gradient
options.why: Glucose is moved against its gradient here. The energy comes indirectly from ATP used at the pump.

options.text: Inside the glucose molecule once it's in the cell
options.why: That's respiration, which happens after transport. The transport step is paid for at the pump.

questions.stem: What opens a ligand-gated ion channel?

options.text: A change in voltage across the membrane
options.why: That's a voltage-gated channel. The two types are told apart by what opens them.

options.text: A specific chemical, such as a neurotransmitter, binding
options.why: A ligand is a signaling molecule. When it binds the channel, the channel changes shape and opens.

options.text: Energy released when ATP is hydrolyzed
options.why: Channels don't use ATP. That's how pumps work.

options.text: A difference in water potential across the membrane
options.why: Water potential drives osmosis. It doesn't open ion channels.

questions.stem: What is the role of glycoproteins on the outer surface of the membrane?

options.text: Pumping ions against their gradients using ATP
options.why: That's pump proteins. Glycoproteins have carbohydrate chains that face outward for recognition.

options.text: Cell recognition and adhesion between cells
options.why: Their carbohydrate chains act as identity markers other cells can recognize, and they help cells stick together.

options.text: Controlling membrane fluidity at low temperatures
options.why: That's cholesterol and unsaturated tails.

options.text: Letting water cross the membrane faster
options.why: That's aquaporins.
